rationale: A wins because it stays inside the fence of the facts and turns missing evidence into useful traps for the founder. Its line, "the 9-minute engagement figure is not outcome data and must not be presented as if it were," is the kind of discipline that prevents a pitch from becoming a correction. B has good shapes, but "Duolingo says engagement is at an all-time high" turns a DAU record into an engagement claim, and that is how slop sneaks into a smart draft.
gaps_in_A: "Duolingo is an engagement engine for learning anything" is a strong strategic thesis from thin supplied evidence; it needs roadmap, retention, or historical non-language proof before the founder says it out loud.
"it's a top-of-funnel move" states Duolingo's motive for free chess as fact. The update gives pricing/access, not intent.
A misses the clean paid-vs-free business-model contrast as its own angle; it spreads that material across the chess and markets angles instead of making the tiering choice the protagonist.
gaps_in_B: "Duolingo says engagement is at an all-time high" is fact drift. The update says DAUs hit a new high, not engagement overall.
"a live public educator critique of gamification" invents freshness. The update only says some educators have publicly criticized gamification; it does not say the critique is current or live.
"two new product bets in the same quarter" and "ahead of earnings" add timing and market context not in the update. That is not color; that is an invoice from the fact-checker.
"compute-heavy conversational AI feature" may be true, but it is not supplied. If the pricing angle needs cost rationale, ask for it instead of smuggling it into the premise.
